Is the read-back the same as the direct pass?

Yes, in the let's non-recursive branch, with one exception. There the let's real pass and dev's direct pass get the same context (the ModuleExp's), the same expected type (p_syn.ty is the signature already desugared by mpat_to_pat, met with syn; desugar_sig ignores its context and changes nothing the second time), the same term and the same flags; only the ancestors list differs. And the elaboration recorded is the one returned on every path that ends in add. The exception is the lift (next row).
Statics.re:2079, Statics.re:2757-2762, ModuleHelpers.re:51-60, Typ.re:615-657, StaticsBase.re:268-277, Statics.re:268

Under a one-member signature the definition is lifted: autolabel_singleton_tuple records the bare analysis but returns (x = raw source). The extra-member module now gives M.x = 1 (dev: its raw source; confirmed by running in ^report(21)); Alexander confirmed 1 is right. A plain value under that signature gives 5 on dev and gets stuck with #2651 (the runs); Alexander accepts that too, since Modules II part 1 makes it stuck and a static error (his comment; below).
A tuple literal under a product signature

The let rearranges a tuple definition to the pattern's labels before analyzing it, so the read-back is the rearranged tuple's elaboration where dev's direct pass analyzed the original. The tuple case rearranges its own elaboration the same way, so the result should match; a test would settle it.
What does the editor see inside the definition now?

The let's records, not the direct pass's. Two differences, neither in the elaboration: the ancestors list has the ModuleExp's id twice, as the body's already did (auto-probes drop adjacent repeats); and inside a function-valued module that does not name itself, the recorded context contains the module's own name, so completion can offer F inside F, where using it is an error. Dev never showed F there. Alexander's flag (question 3) would remove it.

The self-naming arm, yes: that is the second commit's case. The 'no record found' arm looks unreachable: every analysis ends in add at the term's ids, and the map starts empty each run. It is defensive. Codecov's one missed patch line is the fallback's signature arm, Asc(_, typ) => typ, reached by a module with a signature whose definition names the module, or is a fix the user wrote; module F : Int -> Int = fun x -> F(x) in 1 reaches it when run, and reports its error as dev does (the runs). The self-naming arm is also reached by a definition the user wrote with fix (Alexander's finding, next row).

It reads the shape of the let's elaboration. If the let ever wraps its fixpoint differently, the check turns false silently and the error goes away again; only the one test would notice. A flag that tells the let not to try the recursive case (Alexander's suggestion, question 3) would not depend on the shape at all. Found since, by Alexander: the check is also not exact. It matches a fixpoint the user wrote, module m = fix f -> …, which then takes the old second pass: dev's results, without the speed-up (the guard). He and Matthew agree the signal belongs in the let analysis, and the draft follow-up #2717 (Statics: a module binding is a non-recursive let) puts it there: the module's let is told it is not recursive, so there is no shape to read and no names_itself (the guard, What next).

Unchanged in the common case, and more consistent: the record at the definition's id and the elaboration spliced into the program are now the same value. The guard matters here too: without it, a self-naming definition's record would keep the let's patched co-context, which lacks the module's name, beside an elaboration that uses it, so the reuse check would not see changes to that name.

The statics test passes on any static error anywhere in the program, so it does not pin where the error is or what kind. Untested: a function-valued module that does not name itself (module F = fun x -> x + 1 in F(2), 3), the bare value under a one-member signature, and the fallback's signature arm; all three were run with the command-line tool instead (the runs). The bare value's test goes on Modules II part 1. The draft follow-up #2717 (Statics: a module binding is a non-recursive let) pins the self-naming test, and its form under a signature, to one FreeConstructor mark at the inner F, and adds module F = fun x -> x + 1 in F(2), 3, as an evaluator test (question 5). Evaluator tests run without EvalInfo or a previous run, so they never exercise reuse.

Is the output the same? (the description's 6 → 4 warnings)

The PR's description reports hazel analyze -W on all 73 hazel-programs byte for byte the same before and after, except Measured.WARNING: id … not found lines: 6 before and 4 after on docs/reference/modules.hz. Alexander settled which two went, and why (his comment). His three runs each at the base 34f9605ddf and at fa3eef62ce gave 6 and 4 every time, with the rest of the output byte for byte the same. The ids with no source position are minted by autolabel_singleton_tuple, which analyzes fresh terms and records infos with marks at their ids. module M : {let x : Int} = { let x = 1; let y = 2 } goes through the lift: at the base it went through twice, in the expanded let and in the direct pass, and left two copies of its errors in the map; now it leaves one. analyze sorts and dedups every info with marks, so the duplicates showed only as warnings. So the info map loses two orphaned duplicate errors: a small improvement, not a change in output.

The class override at the ModuleExp's id is overwritten by the final add; docs/modules.md still describes the deleted Elaborator; and the lift returns raw source, so any term needing elaboration under a one-member labeled product reaches the evaluator unelaborated (dev's extra-member result is one case). And the lift records error infos at fresh ids with no source position, which is what those warnings were: a dev issue of its own, Alexander notes, not for this PR (his comment).
